text.p: The portrayal of women in British advertisements sparked more than twice as many complaints in 1996 as in 1995, an industry watchdog said on Tuesday, with one lingerie ad alone drawing 321 complaints,

Many British consumers also objected to a poster campaign by the ruling Conservative Party that showed Tony Blair, the opposition Labur Party leader, with demonic red eyes -- which was subsequently banned.

Britain's Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), the industry's self-regulating body for print ads, said in its annual report the number of complaints about advertising fell 6 percent during 1996 to 12,055 from 12,804 in 1995.
But complaints about the images of women in ads more than doubled in 1996 to 846 -- including 321 complaints over a poster ad for Gossards Glossies lingerie -- from 400 in 1995.
The high number of complaints over the Gossards ad "...was inspired largely by a newspaper columnist who urged readers, many of whom admitted they hadn't seen the poster, to complain," the ASA said.

The ad showed a model clad in see-through black bra and briefs reclining on a haystack. The caption read, "Who said a woman can't get pleasure from something soft?" The ASA did not uphold complaints against the ad.
Overall, the number of ads that drew fire rose 9 percent, and the number of ads withdrawn following ASA's investigations rose 40 percent to 720, the trade group said.

The Conservative Party's so-called "demon eyes" poster ad -- which showed Labour leader Tony Blair with demonic red eyes -- sparked 167 complaints, the second-highest number of complaints for a single ad. The ASA told the Conservative Party to withdraw the ad.

The third-most complained about ad was for Nissan's Terrano Outlander four-wheel drive vehicle. The print and poster ads drew 126 complaints. The ads showed the Terrano superimposed over a woman's body that was decorated to simulate hilly terrain. The complaints were upheld.
